options.A: To attract beneficial animals to the plants
options.B: To prevent attack by caterpillars on the plants
options.C: To help the plants make the best use of available resources
options.D: To communicate with other plants across long distances

items.text:
Plant Communication

The discovery that plants use communication has changed our understanding of their surroundings. However, studies have shown that plants can send chemical signals through the soil. animals or disease-causing agents. For instance, when a corn plant is attacked by caterpillars, it can release specific chemicals that warn nearby corn plants. In response, the neighboring corn plants may release a chemical known as MBOA into their tissues, which makes them less palatable to the caterpillars.

Plants also use electrical signals to respond rapidly to environmental changes. Some plants can even detect the presence of other plants through their roots. This allows them to alter their growth patterns to avoid competition.

Despite these discoveries, the study of plant communication is still in its infancy. Researchers are continuously uncovering new ways that plants interact with each other and their environment.

To: Yael Thomas, Policy Director, CFEs
From: Serena Grant
Sent: March 3, 2:09 p.m.
Subject: Interest in energy regulation policy

Dear Ms. Thomas,

I attended your guest lecture yesterday on regulatory frameworks for the oil and gas sector and found your analysis of industry challenges both candid and thought-provoking. As a junior majoring in political science, I'm eager to understand how regulation affects energy markets.

Could we schedule a brief call next week to discuss your experience advising state commissions on drilling permits?

I especially appreciated your comments yesterday on the debate over domestic energy independence and the role of alternative fuels in shaping future infrastructure.

I'm available Monday or Wednesday afternoons but can adjust to your schedule if needed.

Thank you for considering my request—I value your expertise in navigating complex policy arenas.

Best regards,
Serena Grant

items.text:
Blackout Brings Creativity to Finals Week

A sudden power outage during finals week left Smithfield students scrambling for solutions. Students took advantage of their smart-phone flashlights, and university staff provided camping lights for dorm lounges.

"It was stressful but kind of fun," said sophomore Grace Lee.

The blackout lasted six hours, caused by a transformer failure near campus. Dining services offered free coffee, and professors extended deadlines to ease the pressure.

"We made the best of it," said senior Omar Davis, who studied with his bike light. Social media buzzed with photos of candlelit study sessions, turning the inconvenience into a moment of campus unity.

Some students even organized impromptu acoustic concerts on the quad, proving that creativity thrives under constraints.

"It reminded us that community matters more than convenience," said Professor Laura Chen.

By the early morning hours, power was restored, but the evening's events left a lasting impression.
